value: in a giving-up-density experiment, adding wolf body odour made wild raccoon dogs deplete feeding trays more at plots with low wolf encounter rates but less at plots with high wolf encounter rates (odour x encounter-rate interaction)
units: categorical (giving-up density, pellets left of 20, by wolf-odour treatment and wolf encounter rate)
method: field giving-up-density experiment with camera-trap species attribution; Poisson GLMM in glmmTMB with wolf encounter rate, odour treatment and their interaction as fixed effects, study period and session day as covariates, plot as random factor
conditions: wild-sourced free-ranging animals visiting feeding trays at 20 plots at least about 1 km apart in the southeastern part of Białowieża Forest, Poland, outside the national park and nature reserves, 2019; design unit = giving-up density (GUD, dog-food pellets remaining of 20 mixed into gravel in a 70x40 cm tray) per plot-night, attributed to the species filmed foraging the previous night by one camera trap per station; treatment = a 10x10 cm piece of cotton towel kept 21 days in the sleeping area of a captive adult female wolf, frozen at -80 C, fresh piece pegged to a bamboo cane within 0.5 m of the tray each day; control = towel left outdoors on a washing line, handled the same way; three study periods (June-July, August-September, October), two sessions per period with 10 of the 20 plots per session (5 odour, 5 control), plots randomly assigned to sessions and receiving the alternate treatment in the next period; wolf encounter rate was a landscape-scale gradient across plots; 83 usable GUDs in total (54 raccoon dog, 29 red fox); the wolf odour came from one captive wolf, not from wild wolves; raccoon dog n = 54 GUDs; interaction estimate 0.435 (SE 0.117, z = 3.726, p < 0.001), retained after a likelihood-ratio test; at odour plots there was no significant relationship between wolf risk and GUD, with about 9 pieces left in trays in both high- and low-risk areas; at control plots raccoon dogs depleted trays more in areas with high wolf encounter rates; the abstract also states that the frequency of patch visits by both mesocarnivores was unaffected by wolf body odour or landscape encounter rates (raccoon dogs and foxes did not avoid odour plots); the title reports that wolf risk fails to inspire fear

quote: Simulating wolf presence by adding wolf body odour caused raccoon dogs to deplete feeding trays more at locations with low wolf encounter rates, but less at locations with high wolf encounter rates.
note: Classification: behavioural response (foraging depletion) of free-ranging raccoon dogs to a predator body-odour treatment in the field; no chemoreceptor is identified. Whole Abstract sentence, no cut. The response reverses sign across the encounter-rate gradient, so the value is context-dependent and not a simple avoidance; wolf odour was from a single captive wolf and the odour towel and control towel also differ in having been kept in an enclosure versus on a washing line. value: in the same giving-up-density experiment, adding wolf body odour did not change red fox foraging costs at any wolf encounter rate (null)
units: categorical (giving-up density, pellets left of 20, by wolf-odour treatment and wolf encounter rate)
method: field giving-up-density experiment with camera-trap species attribution; the fox GUD model was the reduced version without the interaction term, Poisson GLMM in glmmTMB
conditions: wild-sourced free-ranging animals visiting feeding trays at 20 plots at least about 1 km apart in the southeastern part of Białowieża Forest, Poland, outside the national park and nature reserves, 2019; design unit = giving-up density (GUD, dog-food pellets remaining of 20 mixed into gravel in a 70x40 cm tray) per plot-night, attributed to the species filmed foraging the previous night by one camera trap per station; treatment = a 10x10 cm piece of cotton towel kept 21 days in the sleeping area of a captive adult female wolf, frozen at -80 C, fresh piece pegged to a bamboo cane within 0.5 m of the tray each day; control = towel left outdoors on a washing line, handled the same way; three study periods (June-July, August-September, October), two sessions per period with 10 of the 20 plots per session (5 odour, 5 control), plots randomly assigned to sessions and receiving the alternate treatment in the next period; wolf encounter rate was a landscape-scale gradient across plots; 83 usable GUDs in total (54 raccoon dog, 29 red fox); the wolf odour came from one captive wolf, not from wild wolves; red fox n = 29 GUDs; fox GUDs did not vary with any tested predictor or covariate (coefficients only in Supplementary Table S5); weak overdispersion (dispersion 0.407, p = 0.024) attributed to small sample size; foxes did not avoid odour plots relative to control plots (chi-square 0.267, P = 0.605); sibling result for raccoon dog in the same paper is a significant odour x encounter-rate interaction
